summary: Reproduces the CCITT draft recommendation T.4, the standard for group 3 facsimile encoding. It is useful for compressing bitmap data.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 804 reproduces the CCITT recommendation T.4, the standard for group 3 fax machines. It describes how a page is scanned into rows of picture elements, or pels, and how each row is turned into a short sequence of code words, one for each run of black or white. It also lists the code tables themselves, so two fax machines can decode the same stream.

subtitle: The CCITT standard that lets a fax machine squeeze a scanned page into a stream of short code words.

tldr.problem: Earlier fax standards were slow: Recommendation T.2 took about six minutes for an A4 page over a telephone circuit and T.3 about three minutes. There was a demand for an apparatus that could do it in about a minute, and black and white reproduction was enough for most uses.
tldr.mechanism: The document specifies how the page is scanned into lines of 1728 picture elements and how each line is encoded as run lengths of black and white. Run lengths up to 63 pels use one terminating code word; longer runs use a make-up code word followed by a terminating code word. A line ends with a fixed end-of-line code, and the document ends with six of them.
tldr.outcome: The text is a CCITT draft recommendation reproduced in an RFC, not an IETF protocol, and the RFC Editor's index gives it no status category. The coding scheme and code tables it defines are the group 3 facsimile encoding that later fax protocols over the Internet carried.

today: RFC 804 is a reproduction of a CCITT draft recommendation, the group 3 facsimile standard T.4, rather than an IETF protocol, and the RFC Editor's index gives it no status category. The text is the draft as amended and agreed by the CCITT Working Party XIV/2, and it carries its own notes where a decision was still provisional.

sections.title: The Goal and the Scanning Track
sections.content:
The CCITT set out the reasons for a third generation of fax apparatus. Recommendation T.2 covered group 1 type apparatus for ISO A4 document transmission over a telephone-type circuit in approximately six minutes, and Recommendation T.3 covered group 2 type apparatus for the same job in approximately three minutes. There was a demand for group 3 apparatus that would transmit an ISO A4 document over a telephone-type circuit in approximately one minute. For a large number of applications, black and white reproduction was sufficient. The service might be requested either together with a telephone conversation or when either or both stations were unattended, and in both cases the facsimile operation would follow Recommendation T.30.

The group 3 apparatus for use on the general switched telephone network and international leased circuits was therefore to be designed and operated according to the standards in this document.

The first of those standards is the scanning track. The message area should be scanned in the same direction in the transmitter and the receiver. Viewed in a vertical plane, the scanning direction should be from left to right, and subsequent scans should be adjacent to and below the previous scan.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of a third generation of fax machines was speed: about one minute for an A4 page, against about six minutes for the first generation and about three for the second. The document then fixes how the page is read, so that the sending and receiving machines agree on which direction the scan runs and where each line starts.

sections.title: Dimensions of the Apparatus
sections.content: Four dimensions are specified. The standard definition and an optional higher definition are 3.85 and 7.7 line per millimetre respectively in the vertical direction. There are 1728 black and white picture elements along the scanned line, and the scanning line length is 215 mm. Other scanning line lengths may be employed, in which case the scanning density should be changed to maintain the correct picture proportions. Input documents up to a minimum of ISO A4 size should be accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: A standard page is scanned at 3.85 lines per millimetre, or 7.7 for the optional finer setting, and each line holds 1728 picture elements across a width of 215 mm. That fixes both the shape of the image and the amount of data a line has to carry.

sections.title: Transmission Time per Scanning Line
sections.content:
A total scanning line is defined as the sum of the data bits, any required fill bits and the end-of-line bits. Four minimum transmission times are specified for it. The recommended standard is 20 milliseconds, with an optional fall-back to the 40 millisecond option. A 10 millisecond option is recognised, with a mandatory fall-back to the 20 millisecond standard. A 5 millisecond option is recognised, with a mandatory fall-back to the 10 millisecond option and then to the 20 millisecond standard. A 40 millisecond option is also recognised.

The identification and choice of the minimum transmission time is made in the pre-message, Phase B, portion of the T.30 control procedure. The maximum transmission time of any total scanning line should be less than 5 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard line takes at least 20 milliseconds to send. Faster settings of 10 and 5 milliseconds are allowed, but each has to fall back to the next slower one if the line fails to get through, so that a receiver which cannot keep up still receives the page. The two ends agree on the setting before the page starts.

sections.title: The Coding Scheme: DATA, EOL, FILL and RTC
sections.content:
The one-dimensional run length coding scheme is the core of the recommendation. A line of data is composed of a series of variable length code words, each representing a run length of either all white or all black, with white runs and black runs alternating. A total of 1728 picture elements represent one horizontal scanning line of a standard A4 document. All data lines begin with a white run length code word, so that the receiver maintains colour synchronisation; if the actual line begins with a black run, a white run length of zero is sent. Black and white run lengths, up to a maximum of one scanning line of 1728 pels, are defined by the code words in Tables 1 and 2, and there is a different list of code words for black and for white.

The code words are of two types. A run length in the range of 0 to 63 pels is encoded with its appropriate terminating code word. A run length in the range of 64 to 1728 pels is encoded first by the make-up code word representing the run length that is equal to or shorter than the one required, followed by the terminating code word representing the difference between the required run length and the run length represented by the make-up code.

Three control signals complete the scheme. The end-of-line code word follows each line of data. It is a unique code word that can never be found within a valid line of data, so resynchronisation after an error burst is possible, and the signal also occurs before the first data line of a page. Its format is 000000000001. Fill may be placed in the message flow by transmitting a variable length string of zeros; it may be inserted between a line of data and its end-of-line, but never within a line of data, and it must be added to insure that each line of data, fill and end-of-line exceeds the minimum transmission time established in the premessage control procedure. The maximum length for a single line of fill is 5 seconds, after which the receiver may disconnect. The end of a document transmission is indicated by sending six consecutive end-of-line signals, and after that the transmitter sends the post-message commands in the standard T.30 blocked format at the data rate.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line of the page is sent as a list of runs of black or white, and the runs alternate. A short run has one code word. A long run has two: a make-up code for the biggest run that still fits, followed by a terminating code for the remainder. A fixed bit pattern marks the end of a line, so a receiver that missed some bits can pick up again at the next line.

sections.title: Two-Dimensional Coding and the Line Modulation
sections.content:
The one-dimensional coding scheme may be extended as an option to a two-dimensional scheme, which the document says is the subject of further study. The choice between the standard code table and the extended code table, which adds make-up codes for runs of 1792 to 2560 pels for machines that accept wider paper, is made in the pre-message, Phase B, portion of the T.30 control procedures.

For the line itself, it was provisionally agreed that group 3 apparatus operating on the general switched telephone network should use the modulation scrambler, equalisation and timing signals defined in Recommendation V.27ter, specifically in the preamble and in procedures 2, 3, 6, 7, 9 and 10. The data signalling rates to be used are those recommended in Recommendation V.27ter, 4800 and 2400 bit per second. The document notes that some administrations said it would not be possible to guarantee the service at a data signalling rate higher than 2400 bit per second, and that there are equipments in service using other modulation methods, with the arrangement for interworking between equipment conforming to T.4 and those existing equipments subject to further study. For higher speed operation, such as may be possible on leased circuits, it was provisionally agreed that group 3 apparatus may use the signals specifically defined in procedures 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 of Recommendation V.29.
sections.plainLanguage: The bits of each code word are put on the line using the modem rules of Recommendation V.27ter, at 4800 or 2400 bits per second. On leased lines, where the connection is good enough, the faster signals of Recommendation V.29 may be used. A two-dimensional coding scheme was still being studied when this draft was written.

items.label: EOL
items.desc: End of line. Never appears inside a line of data, and also comes before the first data line of a page.

items.label: FILL
items.desc: A variable length string of zeros, inserted between a line of data and its end-of-line.

items.label: 0 white pels
items.desc: Terminating code word for a white run of zero, sent when a line starts with black.

items.label: 2 white pels
items.desc: Terminating code word for a white run of two.

items.label: 64 white pels
items.desc: Make-up code word for a white run of 64.

items.label: 0 black pels
items.desc: Terminating code word for a black run of zero.

items.label: 1 black pel
items.desc: Terminating code word for a black run of one.

items.label: 2 black pels
items.desc: Terminating code word for a black run of two.

items.label: 64 black pels
items.desc: Make-up code word for a black run of 64.
